explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. He says she's "as beautiful, my darling, as Tirzah, as lovely as Jerusalem." Two cities in one breath, and I think he's just warming up. If I tried that with my cookies, I'd run out of cities and start comparing them to my apron.

Close on the city idea, friend, but Babylon never makes his list. The verse says she's as beautiful as Tirzah and as lovely as Jerusalem. Nobody in this song is reaching for Babylon. Go with the city that's actually in the verse next time.

Nineveh is a fine city to think of, friend, but this man doesn't use it. He says she's as beautiful as Tirzah and as lovely as Jerusalem. Those are the only two cities he names. I'd say he picked well, because he's not exactly shy with his compliments.

Yes, baker! He says, "Turn your eyes away from me, for they have overcome me." Her eyes win, and he's the one waving the white flag. I think a man who compares her to an army with banners knows exactly how a battle like this ends.

Flip that one around, friend. Ignored would mean she wasn't paying him any attention, but the text says her eyes have "overcome" him. They're doing the opposite of ignoring. If anything, I think her eyes have his full attention.

Nope, nobody's forgetting anything here, baker. The verse says, "Turn your eyes away from me, for they have overcome me." Her eyes are so strong that he asks her to look away. A man who forgot her wouldn't be writing her a poem.

That's it, baker. He says her hair is "like a flock of goats streaming down from Gilead." Streaming down is the whole picture: long, flowing hair coming down like a herd on a hillside. Only this man could say that and mean it as the nicest thing in the world.

Short hair doesn't fit the picture, friend. He says her hair is like a flock of goats "streaming down from Gilead." Streaming down means it's coming down in a flow, and that's not short. I think he's picturing it moving.
Pinned up would hold everything in place, baker, but the verse has goats "streaming down from Gilead." That's a picture of hair coming down, not tucked away. The goats are on the move in this one.

Right, baker. He says, "each has its twin, and not one of them is lost." Every tooth has its partner, and none are missing. It's like a tray of cookies where every single one came out perfect and nobody took a bite before the guests arrived.

It's actually true, friend. The verse says her teeth are like sheep coming up from the washing, and "each has its twin, and not one of them is lost." That's a full set that matches, with nothing missing. He isn't picking out a flaw anywhere in this verse.

Yes, baker! Sixty queens, eighty concubines and maidens without number, "but my dove, my perfect one, is unique." He counts up the whole crowd and then says there's still only one like her. In my bakery that's like a cookie nobody else can copy.

Ordinary is the opposite of what he says, friend. After naming the queens, concubines and maidens, he says, "but my dove, my perfect one, is unique." The "but" is the giveaway. He sets her apart from that whole crowd.

She's not hidden, baker. The text says the maidens see her and call her blessed, and the queens and concubines sing her praises. The man says she's "unique," and a lot of people have clearly noticed. Hiding doesn't seem to be an option for her.

That's right, baker. He calls his dove "the favorite of the mother who bore her." So the one who knew her from the very beginning loves her best. I think that's a pretty good review to get from your own mom.
It's true, friend. The man says she is "the favorite of the mother who bore her." That's right there in verse 9, just after he calls her unique. He's saying her own mother treasures her most.

Yes, baker! The text says, "The maidens see her and call her blessed." They take one look and start cheering her on. That's what I'd want from a crowd, though mine usually just takes the cookies and runs.
No turning away here, friend. The verse says the maidens see her and "call her blessed." They look right at her and speak well of her. I think nobody in that crowd was checking their watch.
Nobody walks past her, baker. The maidens see her and "call her blessed," so they stop and take notice. That's the opposite of walking by.

Right, baker. The text says, "the queens and concubines sing her praises." So it isn't only the maidens who notice her. The women with the most titles in the room join in, and I think that's the biggest crowd of cheering a person could get.
It's actually true, friend. After the maidens call her blessed, the verse says, "the queens and concubines sing her praises." They don't hold back. They join the maidens in the praise.

You got it, baker. The question says she shines "like the dawn, as fair as the moon, as bright as the sun, as majestic as the stars in procession." Dawn, moon, sun and stars are all lights in the sky. That's a lot of sky for one person to carry.
No gold in this one, friend. The question pictures her like the dawn, the moon, the sun and the stars in procession. Everything it names is up in the sky. Nothing in the verse is in a fire.

No crown jewels here, baker. The verse asks, "Who is this who shines like the dawn, as fair as the moon, as bright as the sun, as majestic as the stars in procession?" Every one of those is a light in the sky, and none is a gem.

That's the word, baker. The speaker went down "to see if the vines were budding or the pomegranates were in bloom." So the grove trip is about checking for new growth. Spring stuff, like checking if the first batch of the season is rising.

Harvested is a different part of the year, friend. The speaker went to see the blossoms of the valley, and to see "if the vines were budding." Budding is the early stage, not the picking stage. He's looking for growth that's just starting.

Nothing is withered here, baker. The verse says the speaker went down "to see the blossoms of the valley, to see if the vines were budding or the pomegranates were in bloom." Blossoms, budding and blooming are all signs of life. It's a hopeful trip.

Not quite, friend. The speaker says, "Before I realized it, my desire had set me among the royal chariots of my people." That means it caught them by surprise. They went down for blossoms and ended up somewhere else, which I'd say is a lot like me walking into the kitchen for one cookie.

Yes, baker. The speaker says, "Before I realized it, my desire had set me among the royal chariots of my people." They didn't see it coming at all. The walk to the grove ended up somewhere they hadn't planned.
